rules.title: The three parts of the ASM
points: The workspace holds the expression being evaluated right now.
The stack holds bindings: a name and the value in its slot. New bindings go on top.
The heap holds data structures that are too big for a slot: records, Some cells, Cons cells, closures, Java objects and arrays.
A step either simplifies the workspace, pushes or pops stack bindings, or allocates or updates a heap cell.

rules.title: What fits in a stack slot
points: Primitive values live right in the slot: ints, bools, chars, floats and ().
Constructors with no arguments are small enough to live in the slot: None, [] (Nil) and constructors like Center or MouseDown.
Everything else is a reference: the slot holds an arrow to a heap cell.
In Java, int, boolean, char and double live in the slot; every object and array is a reference, and null is a reference that points nowhere.

rules.title: When the heap grows
points: Every record expression { ... } allocates a new heap cell, even if an equal record already exists.
Every Some e and every Cons (or x :: l) allocates a new cell.
A record update { r with x = 5 } copies: it allocates a new record and leaves r alone.
Every fun ... -> ... (and every named function) allocates a closure.
In Java, new allocates an object or array; an array initializer {1, 2} allocates too.
Naming something never allocates: let b = a copies the arrow, not the cell.

rules.title: Bindings and shadowing
points: let x = e evaluates e to a value, then pushes a new binding of x to that value.
Bindings on the stack never change. A second let x = ... pushes another x; the old one is still there, just shadowed.
A variable always means its most recent binding, looking from the top of the stack down.
Only mutable fields in heap cells can change, with r.f <- v (or r := v for refs).

rules.title: Mutable records and refs
points: r.f <- v changes the field in the heap cell that r points to. Every alias of that cell sees the change.
A ref is a record with one mutable field: ref e allocates { contents = e }, !r reads r.contents and r := v writes it.
Two variables are aliases when their slots point to the same heap cell.
Fields not declared mutable can never change after the record is built.

rules.title: Reference equality (==)
points: a == b is true when both values are the same: the same primitive, or arrows to the same heap cell.
Two separately allocated cells are never ==, however equal their contents.
Some a == Some a is false: each Some a allocates its own cell.
Java's == on objects (including Strings and arrays) is reference equality too; on ints it compares values.

rules.title: Structural equality (=)
points: a = b follows arrows and compares the contents all the way down.
Structural equality can change over time if one side is mutated.
On a cyclic structure, = can loop forever; == cannot.
Java has no structural ==. Strings use s.equals(t); arrays need Arrays.equals or a loop.

rules.title: Function calls
points: A function value is a closure in the heap: its code plus the bindings it saved when it was created.
To call f e: evaluate e, save the rest of the workspace on the stack, push the closure's saved bindings, then push the parameter bindings.
When the body is a value, pop everything the call pushed and put the result back into the saved workspace.
Bindings made inside a function (parameters, let ... in, match variables) disappear when it returns, unless a closure saved them.

rules.title: Closures
points: A closure saves a copy of the stack bindings for the free variables of its body (variables it uses but does not define).
Saved bindings are copies of slots: if a saved slot holds an arrow to a mutable record, the closure and others still share that record.
Shadowing a variable after the closure was made does not affect it; the closure kept the old binding.
Parameters and top-level library functions are not saved bindings.
A record of closures that share private state is the OCaml version of an object.

rules.title: Queues and deques in the ASM
points: A queue is a record with head and tail fields; each is None or an arrow to a Some cell that points to a qnode.
Evaluating Some n twice (once for head, once for tail) makes two Some cells pointing to the same node.
q.head <- n.next copies the arrow in n.next: no new Some cell is made.
Queue invariant: (1) head and tail both None or both Some; (2a) tail reachable from head by next; (2b) the tail node's next is None.
Deques add a prev field and two more clauses: (2e) if n.next = Some m then m.prev = Some n; (2f) the mirror for prev.
Check the empty-queue case and the case where the last node is removed: both head and tail must change.

rules.title: Java ASM
points: Each method call pushes a frame with its parameters and local variables; it is popped on return.
Arguments are copied into the new frame. Copying a reference lets the method change the object, but not the caller's variable.
Objects have one cell per field, initialised to 0, false or null if the constructor does not set them.
A 2D array is an array of references to row arrays. Rows can be shared, null, or different lengths.
String literals with the same text share one object; new String("x") always makes a new object.

rules.title: Exam drawing checklist
points: Draw every heap cell the code allocates, including Some cells and closures.
Draw the stack bottom-first in the order bindings were made; keep shadowed bindings.
Put primitives and None/Nil directly in slots and fields; use arrows for everything else.
After a mutation, cross out the old field value and draw the new one.
For "which program builds this picture", count heap cells and check which arrows are shared.

lessons.title: Shadowing pushes a new binding
lessons.summary: A second let x does not overwrite the first x; it pushes a new binding on top.
lessons.code:
let x = 1
let y = x + 1
let x = 10
let z = x + y

steps.note: x is bound to 1.
The workspace evaluates x + 1 using the only x, so y is 2.

ask.prompt: What happens to the slot of the first x when line 3 runs?
choices: Nothing: a new x is pushed
ask.explain: Stack bindings never change. Line 3 pushes another binding named x.

steps.note: A new binding for x goes on top. The old x is still on the stack, but shadowed.

ask.explain: x means the most recent binding (10), and y is still 2, so z = 12.

steps.note: Looking up from the top, x is 10 and y is 2, so z is 12.

lessons.title: Aliasing a mutable record
lessons.summary: Changing a field through one alias is visible through every other alias of the same cell.

steps.note: The record literal allocates a cell; a points to it.
b copies a's arrow: a and b are aliases of one record.
A second record literal allocates a second cell, even though its contents match.

ask.prompt: After line 4, what is a = c?
ask.explain: Structural equality compares contents: both records have count = 1. (a == c is false: different cells.)

steps.note: b.count <- 5 updates the cell b points to, which is the same cell as a.

ask.prompt: After line 5, is a = c still true?
ask.explain: a's record now has count 5 and c's has count 1, so a = c is false.

steps.note: Reading a.count follows a's arrow to the updated cell.

ask.explain: a and b share one record, and it was set to 5 through b.

lessons.title: Refs are records with one mutable field
lessons.summary: ref e allocates { contents = e }; := writes through the arrow, so aliases share the update.
lessons.code:
let r = ref 0
let s = r
;; s := !s + 1
let t = ref !r

steps.note: ref 0 allocates a record { contents = 0 }. r points to it.
s copies r's arrow: both name the same ref cell.

ask.prompt: After line 3 runs, what will !r be?
ask.explain: s and r point to the same cell, so writing through s changes what r sees.

steps.note: !s reads contents (0); s := 1 writes 1 into the shared cell.
!r reads 1, and ref 1 allocates a brand new cell for t.

ask.explain: Both cells hold contents = 1, so they are structurally equal. r == t is false: t is a new cell.

lessons.title: A record update copies the record
lessons.summary: { p with x = ... } allocates a new record; mutating the copy leaves the original alone.

steps.note: p1 points to a new record. Only y is mutable.

ask.prompt: Does { p1 with x = 5 } allocate a new record?
ask.explain: A with-expression builds a fresh record, copying the fields you don't mention.

steps.note: p2 is a new cell: x = 5, and y copied from p1 (2).
Only p2's cell changes.

ask.explain: p1 and p2 are different cells, so p1.y is still 2.

steps.note: p1.y follows p1's arrow to the original record.

lessons.title: A record of closures is an object
lessons.summary: Two closures that save the same ref share private state, like methods of one object.

steps.note: make is a function, so its closure is allocated in the heap. It saves nothing.

heap.label: fun () -> let r = ... in { incr = ...; get = ... }

steps.note: Calling make () pushes no parameters (the argument is ()). The let pushes r, pointing to a new ref cell.

heap.label: fun () -> let r = ... in { incr = ...; get = ... }

ask.prompt: How many heap cells will make () have allocated when it returns?
ask.explain: The ref, two closures, and the record holding them: 4 cells.

steps.note: Each fun saves r (its free variable). The record holds arrows to both closures. make returns, its frame is popped, and o points to the record.

heap.label: fun () -> let r = ... in { incr = ...; get = ... }

steps.note: Each o.incr () runs the incr closure with its saved r, adding 1 to the shared ref twice.

heap.label: fun () -> let r = ... in { incr = ...; get = ... }

ask.explain: get saved the same r that incr updated twice.

steps.note: get reads the same ref cell.

heap.label: fun () -> let r = ... in { incr = ...; get = ... }

lessons.title: Some is its own heap cell
lessons.summary: Every Some e allocates a cell that points at the payload, so two Some a are equal but not ==.
lessons.code:
type counter = { mutable count : int }
let a = { count = 1 }
let o1 = Some a
let o2 = Some a
;; begin match o1 with
   | None -> ()
   | Some x -> x.count <- 7
   end
;; print_int a.count

steps.note: a points to a new record.
Some a allocates a Some cell whose field is an arrow to a's record.

ask.prompt: How many Some cells will there be after line 4?
ask.explain: Each Some a expression allocates its own cell.

steps.note: A second Some cell, pointing at the same record.

ask.prompt: After line 4, what is o1 == o2?
ask.explain: Different Some cells, so == is false. o1 = o2 is true: both contain a record with count 1.

steps.note: Matching Some x pushes x bound to the payload: the arrow to a's record. x.count <- 7 updates that record.
The match is over, so x is popped.

ask.explain: x was an alias for a's record.

steps.note: a still points to the record that was changed through x.

lessons.title: Lists share their tails
lessons.summary: x :: l allocates one Cons cell whose tail is an arrow to the existing list.

steps.note: Each element gets a Cons cell. [] (Nil) is small enough to sit in the last cell's tail field.

ask.prompt: How many new Cons cells does line 2 allocate?
ask.explain: 1 :: l1 makes one cell whose tail points to l1's first cell.

steps.note: One new cell, holding 1 and an arrow to l1. l2 and l1 share the cells for 2 and 3.

ask.prompt: After line 3, what is l2 == l3?
ask.explain: l3 is built from its own three cells. l2 = l3 is true (same elements), but they are different cells.

steps.note: l3 gets three fresh cells, separate from l1 and l2.

lessons.title: Enqueueing onto empty and non-empty queues
lessons.summary: enq allocates a node and Some cells, and the two cases update different pointers.

steps.note: enq is a function value: a closure in the heap.
An empty queue: head and tail are both None, which fits in the fields.
Calling enq 1 q pushes x and q (a copy of the arrow). The let allocates node n with next = None.

ask.prompt: q.tail is None, so the first branch runs. How many Some cells does it allocate?
ask.explain: Some n is evaluated twice, once for head and once for tail.

steps.note: head and tail each get their own Some cell, both pointing at n.
The call returns (), and its frame is popped.
enq 2 q: a new frame, and a new node n2.

ask.explain: q.tail is Some (the node holding 1), so the Some t branch runs with t bound to that node.

steps.note: t is bound to the old tail node. t.next <- Some n links it to n2, and q.tail <- Some n moves the tail. The old tail Some cell is now garbage.

ask.prompt: Is q.head's node the same node as q.tail's now?
ask.explain: head still reaches the 1 node, and tail now reaches the 2 node.

steps.note: The call returns. The queue holds 1 then 2, and the invariant holds: the tail node's next is None.

lessons.title: Dequeueing reuses Some cells
lessons.summary: q.head <- n.next copies an arrow to an existing Some cell instead of allocating a new one.

steps.note: A node for 2 with next = None.
Some n2 allocates a Some cell; the node for 1 points to it.

ask.prompt: How many Some cells will exist after line 6?
ask.explain: One from line 5, plus Some n1 and Some n2 on line 6.

steps.note: The queue record, with two more Some cells: one for head, one for tail.
deq is a closure in the heap.
Calling deq q pushes q; matching Some n binds n to the head node (the 1 node).

ask.prompt: Does q.head <- n.next allocate a new Some cell?
ask.explain: n.next already holds an arrow to a Some cell; the assignment copies that arrow.

steps.note: q.head now points to the same Some cell as the 1 node's next. The old head Some cell is garbage.
n.next is Some, not None, so tail stays as it is.

ask.explain: deq returns n.v, the value of the old head node.

steps.note: deq returns 1; its frame is popped and x is bound to 1. The queue now holds just 2.

lessons.title: A buggy enq that breaks the invariant
lessons.summary: Forgetting to move q.tail leaves a tail node whose next is not None.

steps.note: bad_enq is a closure.
An empty queue.
On the empty queue the first branch is correct: head and tail each get a Some cell pointing at the new node.

ask.prompt: After bad_enq 2 q, which queue invariant will be broken?
choices: (1) head and tail both None or both Some
(2b) the tail node's next is None
ask.explain: The second call links the 1 node to the 2 node but never moves q.tail. tail still reaches the 1 node, whose next is now Some, so (2b) fails. (2a) still holds: the 1 node is reachable from head.

steps.note: t.next <- Some n links the new node, but q.tail still reaches the 1 node. Its next is not None, so invariant (2b) is broken.

lessons.title: insert_head on a deque
lessons.summary: A new head node shares d.head's Some cell as its next, and the old head gets a prev arrow back.

steps.note: insert_head is a closure.
An empty deque.
insert_head 9 d: n is a new node. next = d.head copies None.
d.head was None, so d.tail <- Some n, then d.head <- Some n: two Some cells point at the 9 node. The call returns.
insert_head 18 d: next = d.head copies the arrow to the head Some cell. prev is None.

ask.prompt: Did next = d.head allocate a Some cell?
ask.explain: d.head already holds an arrow to a Some cell; the new node's next copies that arrow.

steps.note: h is the old head (the 9 node). h.prev <- Some n makes it point back to the new node.
d.head <- Some n moves the head to the 18 node. The call returns. Links agree both ways: 18.next reaches 9, and 9.prev reaches 18.

ask.prompt: Following d.tail and then prev, which value do you reach?
ask.explain: d.tail reaches the 9 node, and its prev reaches the 18 node.

lessons.title: == and = on values and records
lessons.summary: Primitives compare by value either way; records are == only when they are the same cell.

steps.note: x holds 5 in its slot.
y holds its own 5.

ask.explain: Primitive values sit in the slots, and == on them compares the values: 5 is 5.

steps.note: A record cell for a.
A separate record cell for b with the same contents.

ask.explain: Two record literals make two cells. a = b is true; a == b is false.

steps.note: c copies a's arrow.

ask.explain: c and a point to the same cell.

lessons.title: Structural equality changes when you mutate
lessons.summary: a = b can flip from true to false and back as fields change; a == b never changes.

steps.note: a points to a record.
b points to a different record with the same contents.
oa points to a Some cell wrapping a's record.

ask.explain: The expression Some a allocates a fresh Some cell, so it is never == to oa. oa = Some a is true.

steps.note: b's record now has count 2.

ask.explain: 1 is not 2.

steps.note: Now both have count 2 again.

ask.explain: The contents match again, so a = b is true. a == b is still false.

lessons.title: What a function call does to the stack
lessons.summary: A call pushes the argument bindings, evaluates the body, then pops them.
lessons.code:
let add (x : int) (y : int) : int = x + y
let z = add 2 3

steps.note: Defining add allocates a closure in the heap. Its body uses only its parameters, so it saves no bindings.

ask.prompt: When add 2 3 starts running, what gets pushed on the stack?
ask.explain: The rest of the workspace is saved, then the parameters x = 2 and y = 3 are pushed.

steps.note: Inside the call: x and y are bound to the arguments. The workspace is the body.
The body is a value, 5. The call's bindings are popped, and z is bound to 5.

lessons.title: A counter with private state
lessons.summary: Each call to make_counter makes a new record and a new closure that saves it.

steps.note: make_counter is a closure.
Calling make_counter () for c1: the let pushes c, pointing to a new record.

ask.prompt: Which bindings will the returned closure save?
ask.explain: Its body uses only c, so it saves a copy of c's binding.

steps.note: The fun allocates a closure that saves c. The call's frame is popped; c1 points to the closure.
A second call makes a second record and a second closure.

ask.prompt: Do c1 and c2 share a counter record?
ask.explain: Each call ran { count = 0 } again, so each closure saved a different record.

steps.note: c1 () pushes c1's saved c, bumps that record to 1, and returns 1.
c1 () again: the same record goes to 2.

ask.explain: c2 saved its own record, still at 0, so c2 () returns 1.

steps.note: c2 () uses the second record.

lessons.title: A closure keeps the binding it saw
lessons.summary: Shadowing a variable later does not change the copy a closure already saved.
lessons.code:
let n = 10
let addn (x : int) : int = x + n
let n = 100
let r = addn 1

steps.note: n is bound to 10.
addn's body uses n, a free variable, so the closure saves a copy of the binding n = 10.
A new binding of n is pushed. The closure still holds its own n = 10.

ask.explain: The closure saved n = 10 when it was created; the later n = 100 is a different binding.

steps.note: The call pushes the saved n = 10, then x = 1. The body is 1 + 10 = 11. Everything is popped and r is bound to 11.

lessons.title: Java objects and aliasing
lessons.summary: A Java variable of class type holds a reference; assigning it copies the reference.

b copies a's reference: one object, two names.
The assignment goes through b's reference to the shared object.
A second, separate object.

lessons.title: Shared rows in a 2D array
lessons.summary: A 2D array holds references to row arrays, so two rows can be the same array.

steps.note: The initializer allocates an int array; row refers to it.

Lines 5 and 6 copy row's reference into both slots. Both rows are the same array.

steps.note: Prints 9 true.
g[1] now refers to a brand new array. g[0] and row still share the first one.

lessons.summary: Strings are objects: == compares references, equals compares characters.

s2 copies the reference.

lessons.title: Method frames and copied arguments
lessons.summary: Arguments are copied into the new frame: a copied reference still reaches the caller's array, but a copied int is independent.

steps.note: main's frame: arr refers to a one-element array.
k is an int, so it lives in its slot.
Calling bump pushes a new frame. a gets a copy of arr's reference; n gets a copy of k's value.
a[0] = a[0] + 1 writes through the copied reference into main's array.

ask.explain: n is bump's own slot holding a copy of the value.

bump returns and its frame is popped.

quizzes.prompt: type counter = { mutable count : int }. After let a = { count = 1 } let o1 = Some a let o2 = Some a, which is true?
quizzes.explain: Two Some cells (so not ==), but both wrap the same record, so they are structurally equal.

quizzes.prompt: How many heap cells are allocated by evaluating this expression once (not counting anything allocated when the functions later run)?
quizzes.code: let r = ref 0 in (fun () -> incr r), (fun () -> !r)
quizzes.explain: The ref cell, two closures, and the pair that holds them: 4 cells. Tuples are heap allocated like records.
